rationales.because: because enterprise deals are strategic, high-value accounts (flagship logos, reference customers, $1M+ ACV deals with executive sponsorship) where winning the customer is judged to be worth giving up margin beyond the 15% policy limit, up to 30%.
rationales.judge_why: Both state the reason is that the deal is a strategic account, specifically an enterprise logo and/or a $1M+ deal. The proposed rationale adds extra detail about value and margin, but the core business reason matches.

rationales.because: because when a deal is genuinely competitive outside France, reps need room to match rivals' pricing to win it, so discounts up to 26% (above the 15% policy) are approved under the standard competitive grid.
rationales.judge_why: Both state that the rationale is competitive displacement/competitive pricing outside France, with France handled separately.

rationales.because: the company rewards long-tenured customers (over 11 years) with a capped exception discount of up to 22%, above the 15% policy, to retain their loyalty and protect the long-term relationship.
rationales.judge_why: Both state that the discount/exception is justified by customer loyalty due to long tenure.

rationales.because: because longer-term renewal commitments (multi-year lock-in, especially 3-year terms) justify giving a larger discount than the 15% policy, as the extra discount is traded for retained, committed revenue and reduced churn risk.
rationales.judge_why: Both state that larger discounts are justified by multi-year renewal commitments, with discount increasing for longer terms and tied to reduced churn risk/retained revenue.

rationales.because: because regional finance sets a stricter margin floor for SMB deals in Germany, capping discounts at 10%, so any deeper discount falls below that floor and is rejected
rationales.judge_why: The proposed rationale states that regional finance set a stricter margin floor for SMB deals in Germany, which is the same business reason as the true rationale.

rationales.because: because large, strategically valuable accounts (big deal size, enterprise flagship or reference customers, long-tenured loyal clients) justify a moderate discount above the 15% policy cap, up to 20%, to win or retain high-value business.
rationales.judge_why: The proposed rationale includes the core TRUE reason that a large deal size justifies a moderate discount, though it adds broader strategic-account context.

rationales.because: because renewals that commit to a multi-year term (over 2 years) lock in recurring revenue and reduce churn risk, so the company accepts a discount above the 15% policy (up to 24%) in exchange for the longer commitment.
rationales.judge_why: Both rationales state that multi-year renewal commitments justify higher discounts because longer terms reduce churn risk and secure recurring revenue; the proposed adds specific policy/discount details but preserves the same business reason.

rationales.because: because customers at high risk of churn who renew on a multi-year term get an above-policy discount (up to 26%), since the longer lock-in commitment is worth more to the company than the lost margin.
rationales.judge_why: Both state that multi-year renewal commitments justify higher discounts, with discounts increasing for longer terms and being greater when churn risk is higher.

rationales.because: the notes give no coherent, consistent business rationale: most are generic approvals ('fine', 'my call', 'I know this account') reflecting individual discretion, and only a couple of outliers hint at strategic deals (board-level $1M+ ACV, competitor displacement) while one note is about a different region and segment.
rationales.judge_why: Both indicate that no legitimate/coherent business rationale was provided, with approvals based on vague individual discretion such as 'my call' rather than a defined business reason.

A general competitive-pressure allowance up to about 30% explains them, including the FR competitor deals. Most of the rows above 30% look like noise or other cases.

Several quarter-end deals were approved at only 15.6–20.5% across MM and SMB, just above the 15% policy. A modest quarter-end push allowance of about 21% fits them, and none of the known rules cover them.

Churn-risk accounts, including non-renewals that the known churn rule misses, were approved at 16.5–23% (e.g. 16.5, 17.3, 18.5, 18.7, 19.1, 20.2, 20.4, 22.7). A retention allowance of about 23% explains these.
